idiom_name: keyword arguments (def m(x:, y: 1)) or a Data.define carrier
implementation_notes: Ruby's keyword arguments are the language's named-argument mechanism: `def draw_edge(x:, y:, width: 1)` reads like the parameter object without introducing a type, and a missing keyword raises `ArgumentError`. When the group must be passed as one value, `Data.define` (Ruby 3.2+) builds an immutable value-alike class with generated accessors, `==`, `to_h` and pattern-matching support, replacing a hand-written parameter class; `Struct` is the mutable alternative, and a plain class remains right when `initialize` must validate.
code_sketch:
DrawParams = Data.define(:x, :y, :width, :height)

def draw_edge(params)
  # params.x, params.y, ...
end

draw_edge(DrawParams.new(x: 2, y: 3, width: 1, height: 8))
pitfalls: `Data`/`Struct` equality is member-wise, so a mutable member makes the carrier unsafe as a Hash key or Set element.
A trailing Hash parameter (`def f(opts = {})`) silently accepts any keys, unlike real keyword arguments - prefer explicit keywords or `**opts` when the shape matters.
Ruby 3 separates keyword arguments from positional hashes, so code that passed a bare Hash to keyword parameters under 2.x now raises ArgumentError.
